entry.title: feat: raise the deck upload limit to 100 MB and make it configurable
entry.content:
feat: raise the deck upload limit to 100 MB and make it configurable

The cap was 64 MB in two places: MAX_BYTES inside the upload server action,
and serverActions.bodySizeLimit in next.config.ts. The second one is the
gate that actually bites, and `next build` serializes it into the standalone
bundle - so reading an env var there would freeze the value into the image
at build time, and the prebuilt GHCR image everyone deploys could never be
re-tuned from docker-compose. An env-configurable limit is not reachable
from a server action at all.

Route handlers carry no such cap, so the upload moves to POST /api/import
and the limit becomes ours to enforce. ANKI_MAX_UPLOAD_MB is read per
request rather than at module load, so a container restart applies it and
no rebuild is involved. It defaults to 100, falls back to 100 with a warning
when it is not a positive number, and clamps at 2048 so a typo cannot ask
the process to buffer more than it can chew.

Three gates, cheapest first. The browser checks file.size before sending,
so a 101 MB mistake never leaves the machine. The route refuses on
Content-Length before reading a byte of the body. The real size is checked
again once the form is parsed, because a header can lie. The drop zone shows
the configured cap, passed down from the server component so no NEXT_PUBLIC_
variable is needed to display a server-side value.

The parsing itself is unchanged - it moved to lib/import/upload.ts, shared
by the route and the CSV re-preview action. bodySizeLimit stays at 64mb
because card attachments still go through an action, and its comment now
says which of the two uploads it governs.

Verified at ANKI_MAX_UPLOAD_MB=2 (3 MB file refused with 413 and a message
naming the variable, a 1.2 KB .apkg still parsed, page rendered "Up to
2 MB") and with the variable unset (page rendered 100 MB, the same 3 MB file
passed the size gate).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: export a deck as .apkg or CSV
entry.content:
feat: export a deck as .apkg or CSV

Decks could come in but never leave, which makes this a place you put
cards rather than a place you keep them. Both formats are downloads from
the deck's settings page.

The .apkg writer targets schema 11 - the last collection format that is
plain SQLite rather than protobuf, and the one modern Anki still accepts
and upgrades on the way in. It carries the notes, tags, a three-field note
type whose template count follows the deck's own reverse setting, the media
files with their <img> and [sound:...] markup rebuilt, and the review log.

Scheduling is where it gets lossy. Schema 11's card columns are SM-2, so
FSRS stability and difficulty have nowhere to live: review cards keep their
interval and due date, and learning cards become reviews rather than being
stranded mid-step, since schema 11 encodes a step's position in `left` and
guessing at it would be worse than not trying. The revlog ships too, which
is what Anki's own FSRS needs to derive memory state again.

Note identity survives the trip. Anki matches notes on guid, not id, so the
guid is derived from the note rather than randomised - export the same deck
twice, import it twice, and Anki updates instead of duplicating.

The CSV writer emits the four columns the importer reads, so a file exported
here comes straight back in. Attachments are listed by filename, and a side
that is only a picture takes its filenames in place of the missing text, so
the row survives instead of being silently dropped.

Verified by opening the package and checking what Anki's importer checks:
all five tables, ver 11, crt on a day boundary, model `req` present (schema
11 packages fail to import without it), 0x1f-separated fields, space-padded
tags, sfld and csum taken from the first field's stripped text, unique
revlog ids, and no orphaned cards or revlog rows. Then the round trip: a
deck exported and imported straight back reports 0 added and every note a
duplicate, which - since the fingerprint includes media content hashes -
means not one byte of any image moved.

Not verified against real Anki, which is not installed here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: import and study images and audio from Anki cards
entry.content:
feat: import and study images and audio from Anki cards

Media was the one part of an .apkg we threw away: stripAnkiHtml counted
the <img> tags and [sound:...] references it deleted, and the UI told you
how many had gone. A picture deck imported as a wall of blank fronts, and
half of it did not import at all, because a note needed two non-empty text
fields to survive.

Store files content-addressed, keyed by the sha256 of their bytes:

  media       one row per distinct file (hash, filename, mime, size)
  note_media  which file sits on which field of which note

A pronunciation clip shared by fifty notes is stored once, and re-importing
a deck costs nothing on disk. Bytes live at <db dir>/media, two hex
characters of the hash deep, so /data already covers them in a backup.
ANKI_MEDIA_DIR overrides the location.

Reading the package needs both manifest formats Anki has shipped: the
legacy JSON index-to-name map, and the zstd-compressed protobuf written
since 2.1.50. The protobuf reader here pulls the one field it needs out of
MediaEntries rather than adding a runtime for it. Members are individually
zstd-framed in the new format, which the frame magic tells us more reliably
than the manifest's own flags do.

A side is now "empty" only when it has neither text nor a file, so a
picture-only front is a card rather than a skipped row. That makes the
old fingerprint wrong: a picture deck whose cards share no text would
collapse to one note. Front and back media hashes now feed into it, in a
way that leaves fingerprints of text-only notes byte-identical, so
existing rows stay valid.

Media is staged on disk beside the parsed result rather than inside its
JSON, since a deck with a few hundred clips is tens of megabytes of base64,
and it only moves into the store once the import is confirmed.

Serving is /api/media/<sha256>.<ext>: immutable, cached forever, and
byte-range capable because Safari will not play an <audio> source that
cannot serve ranges. Uploaded SVGs are scriptable, so the response carries
a default-src 'none' sandbox for anyone who opens the raw URL. The service
worker treats these like hashed build output and steps aside for range
requests, which cannot go into the cache.

Studying plays a side's audio when that side appears, the way Anki does,
with a speaker button to replay. The add and edit forms take files per
field, and a side with an attachment stops demanding text. Removing an
attachment, deleting a note or deleting a deck prunes any file nothing
points at any more.

Two fixes that the media path made load-bearing: import warnings were
painted in a hardcoded light-mode ink on a themed background, unreadable
in dark mode and now shown for every media deck, and the import page still
promised that media would be dropped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: ci: build amd64 only
entry.content:
ci: build amd64 only

Measured on the v0.1.2 build: amd64 took 85s of step time, the emulated
arm64 layer took 399s - 4.7x slower, with `npm run build` going from 24s to
234s and `npm ci` from 24s to 141s. The whole run was 10m36s and arm64 was
the critical path for all but 74 seconds of it.

The only host this image is deployed to is x86_64, so the arm64 layer was
paying five minutes a release for nothing. The workflow comment says how to
put it back if that ever changes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

owl and a badge row up top, the deck list as a hero image, then study,

bottom-left of the UI.

entry.title: fix: centre the text in inputs
entry.content:
fix: centre the text in inputs

The coss Input renders a wrapper span around the real control, so the
h-12 class every call site passed was sizing the span while the inner input
kept its own h-8.5/leading-8.5. The text ended up sitting near the top of a
48px box.

Give the component proper duo and duo-sm sizes instead, so the height and
line-height land on the control that actually renders the text, and drop the
height overrides from all 13 call sites. The inner control now measures 48px
with a 48px line-height, 2px inside the border on both edges.

Also pins the inner text to 16px at every breakpoint, which stops iOS
zooming the page in when a field is focused - worth having in an app meant
to be installed on a phone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: ci: publish semver image tags and decouple latest from main
entry.content:
ci: publish semver image tags and decouple latest from main

Every push to main was moving :latest, so a "Pull and redeploy" could land
on any half-finished commit. Version the packages instead:

  tag v0.1.0  ->  0.1.0, 0.1, latest, sha-<short>
  push main   ->  edge, sha-<short>

{{major}} is omitted on purpose - a bare `0` tag would span breaking changes
while the project is pre-1.0.

package.json is the version of record and CI fails a tag that disagrees with
it, so a mislabelled image cannot be published by accident.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix: explain SQLITE_CANTOPEN instead of throwing a stack trace
entry.content:
fix: explain SQLITE_CANTOPEN instead of throwing a stack trace

Mounting a host directory the container user cannot write to is the most
likely way to get this wrong: Docker creates a missing bind-mount directory
as root, while the image runs as uid 1000. SQLite then fails with
SQLITE_CANTOPEN and the log gives no hint about ownership.

Check the directory is writable before opening the database, and on failure
log which uid owns it, which uid the process runs as, and the chown command
that fixes it (plus the SELinux :z case).

Also document adding the service to an existing compose stack, where bind
mounts make this the default outcome rather than the exception.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: ci: publish the image to GHCR and document Portainer deploys
entry.content:
ci: publish the image to GHCR and document Portainer deploys

Building on the server is slow and needs ~2 GB of RAM, so build in Actions
instead and let the server pull.

- Workflow builds linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 on every push to main and
  pushes ghcr.io/<repo>:latest, authenticating with the built-in
  GITHUB_TOKEN - no secrets to configure.
- docker-compose.portainer.yml is a paste-ready stack for Portainer's web
  editor. It binds to all interfaces, which is fine on a tailnet or LAN and
  is called out as the thing to narrow if that stops being true.
- README covers both routes (pull vs build-from-git), the GHCR package
  visibility step, and why the PWA needs HTTPS to install - with
  `tailscale serve` as the one-liner for a tailnet.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix: escape the NUL separator in the note fingerprint
entry.content:
fix: escape the NUL separator in the note fingerprint

The separator between the normalized front and back was a literal 0x00
byte in the source, which made git treat fingerprint.ts as a binary file
(no diffs, and a hazard for editors that strip NULs).

Written as a unicode escape the file is plain ASCII again and the hashed
bytes are identical, so existing fingerprints still match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat: build lexo, a self-hosted spaced-repetition PWA
entry.content:
feat: build lexo, a self-hosted spaced-repetition PWA

A flashcard app with FSRS scheduling, deck import and study stats, backed
by a single SQLite file. Language-agnostic: a deck is a front, a back and
two free-form language labels.

Stack
- Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack, server actions), standalone output
- coss.com/ui (Base UI + Tailwind v4) installed via its shadcn registry,
  re-themed to the Duolingo spec vendored as DESIGN.md
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 + Drizzle, migrations applied on first access
- ts-fsrs for scheduling, shared by the server (authoritative grading) and
  the client (the interval hints on the grade buttons)

Features
- Study sessions with four grades, learning-step requeues inside a session,
  keyboard control (Space to flip, 1-4 to grade) and a completion screen
- Deck CRUD, inline card authoring, card browser with search, suspend,
  reset and delete
- Import from Anki .apkg (schema 11 and 18, zstd collections, deck
  hierarchy, HTML flattening) and from CSV/TSV with a column mapper;
  duplicate notes are fingerprinted and skipped
- Stats from the append-only review log: streak, XP, year heatmap, due
  forecast, retention, rating mix, per-deck totals
- Installable PWA: manifest, maskable icons, shell-caching service worker
  with an offline fallback. Card data is never cached - server-side SQLite
  stays the single source of truth
- Multi-stage Dockerfile and compose file with a /data volume and a
  health check

Design
DESIGN.md is the visual source of truth: Feather Green as the only primary
CTA color, the five-accent gamification vocabulary, and the flat-color drop
shadow that trims on press rather than fading. Dark mode follows the
published dark guidance in section 12.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
